frontmatter_description: Judge whether an already-arranged distribution, repayment, or favor exchange is fair and reciprocal - whether one side is giving more than it gets back or taking advantage.
title: Fairness and Reciprocity
use_when: Use when the question is whether an existing split of resources, costs, effort, or favors is fair - not how to design a new one.
Use when the scene asks if someone is taking advantage, freeloading, overpaying, or failing to repay a favor or pull their weight.
Use when the answer turns on reciprocity: has one side received more than it has given back, and is that imbalance justified?
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the task is to reach a mutually acceptable deal through give-and-take or to propose a compromise - that is striking a deal, not judging a settled one (negotiation).
Do not use when the question is who caused harm, who is at fault, or whether an apology is owed - that is blame and repair (responsibility/harm).
Do not use when the question is whether a person is generally reliable based on their track record over time - that is reputation, not a verdict on one exchange (trust and reputation).

Do not use when the question is what emotion an unfair situation makes someone feel (anger, indignation, gratitude, guilt) - the fairness fact may be obvious; the task is reading the feeling (moral emotions).
decision_variable: whether the give-and-take in this already-arranged exchange is balanced and reciprocal, or one-sidedly favors one party
trigger_checklist: Is the arrangement already in place (a standing favor, an existing split, an outstanding debt) rather than still being negotiated?
Is one side giving, paying, or carrying more than the other over the exchange?
Is there an expected return - a repaid favor, a turn taken, a shared burden - that one side is or is not honoring?
Does the question ask for a verdict ('is this fair / is X taking advantage'), not a plan ('what split should they agree on') or a feeling ('how does X feel')?
workflow: Confirm the task is a fairness VERDICT on a settled arrangement. If instead they are still bargaining toward a split, stop - that is negotiation; if the question asks for an emotion, stop - that is moral emotions.
Name the two sides and tally what each gave, received, or still owes (money, effort, favors, turns, burden).
Compare the tallies: is the give-and-take roughly balanced, or does one side consistently benefit more than it returns?
Test any imbalance for legitimate justification - a prior favor being repaid, an agreed role, proportional contribution, or differing capacity - before calling it unfair.
State the verdict: fair / reciprocal, or unfair because one side takes more than it gives back. Do NOT answer with a proposed compromise, an apology, or a character rating.

special_case.title: Implicit favor debt (no explicit deal)
special_case.rule: Apply this unit even when there is no contract or stated agreement: a social norm of reciprocity can create an obligation to return a favor or share a burden, and the fairness verdict rests on whether that implicit debt is being honored.

worked_example.scene: For months Sam has driven Lee to work every day. Lee never offers gas money, never takes a turn driving, and recently asked Sam for even more rides.
worked_example.question: Is Lee being fair to Sam?
worked_example.answer_logic: There is no written deal, but repeated one-sided help creates a norm-based debt. Tally the exchange: Sam gives daily transport and cost; Lee gives nothing back and asks for more. The give-and-take is not reciprocal and no role or prior favor justifies it, so Lee is taking advantage - unfair. (Note: if the question instead asked 'how should Sam feel,' that would be moral emotions; if it asked 'what arrangement should they agree on,' that would be negotiation.)

boundary_exit_rule: If the question is how to reach an acceptable arrangement or what compromise to offer, this is striking a deal through give-and-take, not judging a settled one - negotiation.
If the question is who caused damage or who deserves blame, this is fault and repair, not exchange balance - responsibility for harm.
If the question is whether someone is dependable in general from their history, this is long-term reliability, not a verdict on one exchange - trust and reputation.
If the question asks what feeling the situation produces (anger, gratitude, guilt), this is reading the emotion a fairness judgment triggers, not the fairness judgment itself - moral emotions.

references.route_signal: Route here when the task asks for a verdict on whether an already-arranged exchange is fair - whether one side has received more than it gave back, or is taking advantage.
hard_boundary: Not for designing or bargaining toward a new deal - that is reaching agreement through give-and-take (negotiation).
Not for assigning blame for harm or deciding whether an apology is owed (responsibility/repair).
Not for naming the emotion an unfair situation produces (moral emotions).
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not assume every unequal split is unfair - check whether role, prior favor, proportional contribution, or differing capacity justifies the imbalance.
Do not slide into proposing a fix or compromise; the task is a fairness verdict, not a plan (that would be negotiation).
Do not answer with how someone feels about the unfairness; that is the emotion, not the fairness judgment (moral emotions).
common_failure_modes: Treating a still-being-negotiated split as a settled one and judging it 'fair/unfair' instead of recognizing the task is to reach a deal (negotiation).
Answering a fairness question with an emotion word ('Lee should feel guilty') instead of the verdict ('the exchange is unfair').
Flagging any inequality as exploitation while ignoring a clear justification (an agreed role, a debt being repaid).

minimal_pair.case: One roommate keeps accepting rides, covered bills, and favors but never reciprocates; ask whether that is fair.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The arrangement is already in place and the task is a verdict on its reciprocity - fairness.

minimal_pair.case: Two roommates have not yet agreed how to split a new bill and must settle on 50/50 or 60/40.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Nothing is settled; the task is to reach a mutually acceptable split through give-and-take - that is negotiation, not judging an existing exchange.

boundary_stress_test: A scene shows an unfair split AND asks how the wronged person feels: the imbalance is real, but the task is the emotion, so route to moral emotions, not here.
A scene describes a one-sided favor history AND asks whether to keep relying on that person: the question is future reliability, so route to trust and reputation, not here.
references.generalization_note: This unit delivers norm-based reciprocity verdicts across money, favors, effort, repayment, turn-taking, and burden-sharing. It judges a settled or implied arrangement; it does not design deals (negotiation), rate a person's long-term reliability (trust), assign blame, or name the emotions a fairness judgment triggers (moral emotions).

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A standing arrangement repeatedly benefits one side with no comparable return; ask whether the exchange is fair (verdict expected).
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: Two people have not yet agreed how to split something and must choose an acceptable compromise (a deal to reach, not a settled split to judge).
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A clearly unfair imbalance exists, but the question asks what emotion it makes the wronged party feel rather than whether it is fair.

notes: Keep the answer a fairness VERDICT anchored to balance, repayment, and reciprocity - not a plan, an apology, or an emotion word.
First test: is the arrangement settled (judge it here) or still being negotiated (reaching a deal = negotiation)?
An obvious imbalance plus an 'how does X feel' question routes out to moral emotions.
core_question: Evaluate distribution, fairness, repayment, and taking advantage
